title: Develop a foal from weanling to yearling

lessons.title: Feeding and managing the weanling
lessons.html:
A critical growth period

Between weaning (about 4 to 6 months) and its first birthday, a young horse grows rapidly. In South Africa, Thoroughbreds all turn a year older on the official birthday (1 August), and yearling sales such as those held in the Western Cape and KwaZulu-Natal mean many youngsters are prepared for sale in this period. Good management now shapes soundness for life.

Nutrition

  • Forage first: good pasture or quality hay such as lucerne mixed with grass hay.
  • Balanced concentrate: a ration made for youngstock, providing protein (especially the amino acid lysine), calcium, phosphorus, copper and zinc in the right balance.
  • Steady growth: avoid both underfeeding and overfeeding. Sudden spurts after periods of poor feeding are linked to developmental orthopaedic disease (DOD), such as physitis and OCD.
  • Feed by weight and condition; adjust amounts as the youngster grows. Use a weigh tape or scale monthly.
  • Fresh water always; salt and mineral licks as advised.

Grouping and environment

  • Keep weanlings in small groups of similar age and size; separate colts from fillies by about 9 to 12 months, or earlier if colts are boisterous.
  • Daily free exercise in large, safe paddocks builds strong bone and tendons. Avoid forced exercise like long lunging on young joints.
  • Safe fencing with no wire or gaps; shade and shelter.
  • An older, quiet "nanny" horse in the group teaches manners.

Health care

  • Vaccinations and boosters as the vet plans, including African horse sickness.
  • Deworming based on faecal egg counts and the vet's programme.
  • Farrier every 4 to 6 weeks to keep feet balanced and to correct limb issues while growth plates are open.
  • Dental check by the vet within the first year.
  • Watch for injuries, swollen joints, lameness and weight loss.

lessons.title: Handling, education and yearling preparation
lessons.html:
Building good manners

Young horses learn quickly. Consistent, calm handling now produces a safe, trainable adult.

  1. Leading: walk at the shoulder, stop and start on voice command, turn both ways, back up a few steps.
  2. Standing tied: short periods tied with a quick-release knot or to baling twine, supervised.
  3. Feet: lifts and holds each foot for picking out and the farrier.
  4. Grooming and touch: accepts handling all over, including ears, mouth and between the hind legs.
  5. Desensitisation: spray bottles, clippers sound, plastic bags, hosepipe, rugs, all introduced gradually.
  6. Loading: practise walking into a horsebox calmly before the first real trip.

Keep sessions short (10 to 15 minutes), end on a good note, reward calm behaviour with release and a scratch, and never allow nipping, barging or kicking to be rewarded.

Monitoring development

MeasureWhy
Body weight and heightCheck steady growth
Body condition scoreNot too fat or thin
Limb conformationSpot deviations early for the vet and farrier
BehaviourProgress in handling

Record all findings monthly in the young horse's file with photos.

Preparing yearlings for sale or show

  • Begin a preparation programme some weeks before the sale: controlled walking exercise, improved grooming and conditioning feed as advised.
  • Teach the youngster to stand square and walk out confidently in hand for inspection.
  • Ensure identification and documents are correct: microchip, passport, vaccination records and breed society registration.
  • Avoid over-fattening; buyers and vets look for an athletic, well-grown youngster.

Key points

  • Aim for steady growth with balanced forage-based feeding.
  • Avoid feeding extremes that cause developmental orthopaedic disease.
  • Free exercise in safe paddocks builds sound legs; avoid forced exercise.
  • Regular farrier, vet and dental care while growth plates are open.
  • Short, consistent handling sessions build good manners.
  • Prepare sale yearlings with conditioning, in-hand training and correct papers.
